raw_response:
*I close my eyes and think about the year ahead...*

---

Thirty-five years I've been doing this. My hands know what to do before my head does. Let me tell you how I'll manage this year.

**Wheat** — I'll plant in the first ten days of October, like always. Eight mu, same fields as last year. I buy seed from the shop in town, the same variety my neighbor Old Wang uses — his wheat always looks good. Before planting, I hire the tractor man from the village to till, and I put down one bag of compound fertilizer per mu at the same time. In March, around when the plants start growing fast again, I'll put down half a bag of urea per mu. I always look at the color — if the leaves go yellow I add a little extra. Irrigation: I water right before the ground freezes in November (the winter water), again when the plants are jointing in March, and again when the heads are filling. Three times. If the spring is dry like last year, maybe a fourth. For pests, I spray once for aphids usually, and I do a herbicide pass in early spring. The combine comes to our village in early June — I don't have to worry about that, I just pay them.

**Maize** — The day after the combine leaves my field, I'm out there planting maize. I can't wait. If I wait a week the season gets short. I broadcast a little compound fertilizer and hire the maize planter from the village cooperative. In July when the plants are tall as me, I scatter urea between the rows by hand — that's the important feeding. Maize doesn't need much from me after that. The combine comes back in September. I usually irrigate once in the summer if there's no rain, maybe twice.

**Cotton** — Four mu on the south side of the village. I start the seedlings inside in April, transplant them to the field around May 1st. Cotton is the hardest work. I spray for bollworm and aphids — you have to watch carefully. I put down compound fertilizer at transplanting and then more when the bolls are setting. Water twice during the season. From September until October, I'm out picking every week, sometimes twice a week. My daughter-in-law helps. Last year cotton prices were not good. My son says I should stop growing it. But I know cotton. And I can sell it right here without going far to market.

My husband does day labor in town, so during peak times it is mostly me and my daughter-in-law. Cotton harvest time is the hardest — we pick by hand, load after load. I may hire two extra people from the next village for ten days.
